# Acknowledgements: the prior work IM stands on

The owner, 2026-10-26 18:44Z: "We are giving everyone access to DMP through Apache 2.0, if any prior work can be used to help
build/improve it, we should use it and thank them kindly." And: "It also has to be Apache 2.0." The two rules are Gravity's
(`vendor/gravity/docs/acknowledgements.md`): use prior work and say so, where it is used; and whatever enters the repository is Apache 2.0
or a licence Apache 2.0 can carry, anything else goes to the owner first. Ideas and papers need no licence; they are cited and thanked.

## Ideas and papers

| Work | What we took | Where it is used | Thanks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Butler W. Lampson, "Protection", *Fifth Princeton Symposium on Information Sciences and Systems* (1971), 437–443; reprinted *ACM Operating Systems Review* 8(1) (1974) | The access matrix: subjects × objects with a set of rights per cell; a capability list is its row. A token's permission list is one row, and the rights alphabet is read, write, execute. | `docs/language.md`; `proof/Im/Grammar.lean`, `Laws.lean` (`Kind`, `Grants`) | The three verbs were already on the page in 1971. |
| Jack B. Dennis and Earl C. Van Horn, "Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations", *Communications of the ACM* 9(3) (1966), 143–155 | The capability: an unforgeable (name, rights) pair; a process acts only through the capabilities it holds. A token is a capability list. | `docs/language.md` | The vocabulary of "a token names the nouns and the rights". |
| Michael A. Harrison, Walter L. Ruzzo and Jeffrey D. Ullman, "Protection in Operating Systems", *Communications of the ACM* 19(8) (1976), 461–471 | Safety is undecidable for the general access matrix even with a fixed rights alphabet; it is the restriction on how authority moves that makes it decidable. So the closure is proven over a closed table of kinds, tokens that only attenuate, and no command that creates authority. | `docs/language.md` (the grammar is closed); `proof/Im/Closure.lean` | The negative result that fixes the shape of what can be proved. |
| Anita K. Jones, Richard J. Lipton and Lawrence Snyder, "A Linear Time Algorithm for Deciding Security", *FOCS* (1976); Lipton and Snyder, *Journal of the ACM* 24(3) (1977), 455–464 | Take-grant: with a fixed small rule set, "can this part acquire this right" is decidable in linear time. The kernel's decision over the generated space is the same idea in a prover. | `proof/Im/Closure.lean` | Decidability by a fixed rule set, fifty years old. |
| Ravi S. Sandhu, "The Schematic Protection Model", *Journal of the ACM* 35(2) (1988), 404–432; "The Typed Access Matrix Model", *IEEE S&P* (1992) | Typed subjects and objects, attenuating creation, acyclic creation graphs: the conditions under which safety stays decidable. Kinds are the types here; grants only attenuate (T24). | `docs/language.md` | The conditions we keep so the proof stays a decision. |
| Butler Lampson, Martín Abadi, Michael Burrows and Edward Wobber, "Authentication in Distributed Systems: Theory and Practice", *ACM Transactions on Computer Systems* 10(4) (1992), 265–310 | Compound principals: A ∧ B says s exactly when both do. The dual gate is the principal Doppler ∧ the operations master, and T1's intersection is its meet. | `proof/Im/Laws.lean` (`decideSentence`, `pass_needs_both_grants`) | The two witnesses as one principal. |
| Dorothy E. Denning, "A Lattice Model of Secure Information Flow", *Communications of the ACM* 19(5) (1976), 236–243 | Already Gravity's: verdicts form a lattice and the gate is a meet. Here its dual: permission sets ordered by inclusion, the intersection as the meet. | `proof/Im/Laws.lean` | The same meet in two lattices. |
| Rob Pike, Dave Presotto, Ken Thompson, Howard Trickey and Phil Winterbottom, "The Use of Name Spaces in Plan 9", *Operating Systems Review* 27(2) (1993), 72–76; Pike et al., "Plan 9 from Bell Labs", *Computing Systems* 8(3) (1995); the 9P2000 manual pages (Plan 9 Foundation, MIT) | Every resource is a name in a hierarchy, one protocol speaks to all of them, and control is a write to a control file: a named verb people type is one write sentence, not a fourth verb. "A walk in a directory is regarded as executing the directory, not reading it." | `docs/language.md` (nouns as paths, the spellings) | The idea that a protocol needs read, write and naming, and nothing else. |
| Rob Pike and Dennis M. Ritchie, "The Styx Architecture for Distributed Systems", *Bell Labs Technical Journal* 4(2) (1999), 146–152 | The same file interface served on every platform without per-platform code: evidence that `cm.ii.file` needs none. | `docs/language.md` (cm.ii and cm.os) | Inferno did it on every machine it ran on. |
| Dennis M. Ritchie and Ken Thompson, "The UNIX Time-Sharing System", *Communications of the ACM* 17(7) (1974); the Multics access control lists (Daley and Neumann 1965; Saltzer 1974) | The rights alphabet r, w, x on files and its origin; execute on a container is traverse. | `docs/language.md` | Where the three letters come from. |
| Mark S. Miller, "Robust Composition: Towards a Unified Approach to Access Control and Concurrency Control", PhD thesis, Johns Hopkins (2006) | The object-capability discipline: authority is only what a reference lets you do, no ambient authority; a membrane as the pattern an MCP facade over cm.ii must follow. | `docs/language.md` ("What is not here yet", the MCP facade) | The discipline the facade will keep. |
| Thomas Sewell, Simon Winwood, Peter Gammie, Toby Murray, June Andronick and Gerwin Klein, "seL4 Enforces Integrity", *ITP* (2011); Toby Murray et al., "seL4: from General Purpose to a Proof of Information Flow Enforcement", *IEEE S&P* (2013) | A capability derivation tree where a derived capability's rights are a subset; machine-checked integrity. The shape "one lemma per command, one fold theorem" for the lemma ledger. The seL4 proofs are GPL-2.0-only and nothing of them enters here; the shape is cited, not copied. | `docs/language.md` ("the lemma ledger") | Rights that only attenuate, proven for a whole kernel. |
| Kyndylan Nienhuis et al., "Rigorous engineering for hardware security: Formal modelling and proof in the CHERI design and implementation process", *IEEE S&P* (2020) | Capability monotonicity proven over a whole instruction set by induction over the finite command set: the same shape as the closure over a finite grammar. | `proof/Im/Closure.lean` | The proof shape for "every command keeps the invariant". |
| Joseph W. Cutler et al., "Cedar: A New Language for Expressive, Fast, Safe, and Analyzable Authorization", *OOPSLA* (2024), DOI 10.1145/3649835; Craig Disselkoen et al., "How We Built Cedar: A Verification-Guided Approach", arXiv:2407.01688 (2024); the Lean model `cedar-policy/cedar-spec` (Apache 2.0) | Verification-guided development: an executable model in Lean with proven properties, and the production engine differentially tested against it. The committed shape table replayed by the C# tests is that method at IM's size; the Thm-folder layout of one file per property family is followed in `proof/Im/`. Nothing of Cedar is copied; the method and the layout are. | `proof/tools/check.sh` (the table), `tests/Language/ShapeTableTests.cs`, `docs/language.md` | A production authorization language proven in Lean, open, and honest about what tests still find. |
| Arnar Birgisson et al., "Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats", *NDSS* (2014); the Biscuit specification (Eclipse Foundation, Apache 2.0); SPKI certificate theory, RFC 2693 (1999) | Tokens that only attenuate: a holder may narrow a grant, never widen it; two grants in a chain reduce to their intersection. Macaroons are symmetric-key and so not taken as a format (C19 needs two keys); the attenuation discipline is. | `docs/language.md` (grants only attenuate) | The discipline of narrowing. |
| The Fuchsia `fuchsia.io` rights (BSD) and Capsicum (Robert N. M. Watson et al., *USENIX Security* 2010; FreeBSD `rights(4)`, BSD); WASI `wasi-filesystem` (W3C Community Group) | A handle carries rights that a derived handle can only lose; a path is resolved relative to a handle and sandboxed to it. The shape of `cm.ii.file` as a capability with read, write and execute, no ambient authority. | `docs/language.md` (the file layer) | File access as a capability, three times over. |
| Model Context Protocol, specification 2025-06-18 (a Series of LF Projects, MIT) | Resources are reads, tools are writes or executes, and the tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`) are the RWX class a tool carries; the facade maps each cm.ii interface onto them. | `docs/language.md` ("What is not here yet") | The surface the facade will speak. |

## How to add an entry

When a file takes an idea from the literature, write it in the file's "Prior art" paragraph with author, title, venue and year, and add
one row above: what was taken, where it is used, and a line of thanks. When a tool or a piece of code is taken in, check its licence
first (Apache License 2.0, or one the Apache License 2.0 can carry); anything else goes to the owner before it enters.
